newsitem.title: USA: Penthouse magazine says U.S. military ban is censorship.
newsitem.headline: Penthouse magazine says U.S. military ban is censorship.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
A Penthouse magazine lawyer argued on Tuesday that a new law banning the sale of sexually explicit material at U.S. military stores constitutes censorship and violates the First Amendment.

"This statute is an attempt to eliminate material from sale on military bases which depicts sex as fun," said Michael Bamberger, whose law firm represents Penthouse's parent General Media Communications Inc.
Penthouse is the third most popular periodical sold at military exchanges in the United States.

General Media and a group of trade associations sued the Department of Defence in October to block enforcement of the Military Honour and Decency Act that restricts the dissemination of "sexually explicit material" within the U.S. military. General Media presented oral arguments in its case during a hearing in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday.

The law was enacted on Sept. 23, 1996 when it was signed by President Bill Clinton. It had been scheduled to take effect on Dec. 22, but U.S. District Judge Shira Scheindlin issued a restraining order on Dec. 20 temporarily blocking the Defence Department from enforcing the provisions.
She ordered the U.S. Defence Department not to change its existing selling policies until she decides whether to issue a preliminary injunction as requested by Penthouse.
The act's provisions prohibit the sale or rental of such material on property controlled by the Defence Department including commissaries and ship stores.
It also bans the sale or rental of such material by a member of the Armed Forces or a civilian officer or employee acting in an official capacity.
The plaintiffs sued the Defence Department alleging that the act violates its First Amendment rights to disseminate constitutionally-protected periodicals, audio and visual recordings.

They argue that the military can only restrict materials covered by the First Amendment when its goal is to protect its ability to carry out its mission and to maintain loyalty, discipline and morale in the armed forces.
Bamberger, a partner with Sonnenschein Nath & Rosenthal, argued that the statute is not related to these goals.
Instead he said the case is about congressional censorship of expression protected by the First Amendment because "congress does not like what they see."
Daniel Alter, assistant U.S. attorney, said the case is about protecting morale in the military.

"The statute is not about 'sex is fun.' The statute is about restricting speech that may express such a message in vulgar and base terms," he said explaining this would "undermine the core values of honour and professionalism considered central to the military."
